passage:
Age nine: Darshan's ball smashed the pantry window. Nearby, some older boys had just been caught spray-painting a wall. 'It's only one pane,' he told the caretaker. 'Look what they did, that's really bad.' The caretaker fixed him with a look and handed him a broom. Darshan swept the glass and later put his pocket money in the repair jar.

Age fifteen: Trisha told her mother she was at the library when she had gone to the mall with friends. At dinner she thought, 'It's just a small lie. Half the girls in my class do much worse, sneaking out at night and worse.' The thought made her feel almost noble. But her mother's soft question, 'How was the library?' stuck in her throat, and she said, 'Actually, I wasn't there.'

Age twenty: Karthik paid a stranger online to write his sociology assignment. 'It's one paper,' he told his roommate. 'People buy entire degrees.' He noticed that the comparison felt comfortable, and then noticed his own name was going on someone else's work. He deleted the file, emailed the professor to ask for an extension, and stayed up to write it himself.

qa.q: What did the caretaker hand Darshan?
How did the comparison with worse acts appear at nine, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: Darshan pointed at older boys who painted a wall, Trisha said half the girls in her class do much worse, and Karthik said people buy entire degrees. Each used a worse example to make a small wrong seem minor instead of judging the act by their own values.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when her mother asked, 'How was the library?'
qa.a: Guilt: the question stuck in her throat and the noble feeling faded, so she told the truth.

qa.q: What made Karthik's change of course work?
qa.a: He noticed that the comparison felt comfortable, saw his name going on someone else's work, and chose to write it himself and ask for an extension.

grounding: Comparing with worse acts to shrink one's own wrongdoing at nine, fifteen and twenty, from a broken window to a lie to a bought assignment.
